# Ring of Nestor

## Lead

The **Ring of Nestor** is a gold signet ring associated with the Mycenaean and Minoan cultural spheres and catalogued in the *Corpus der Minoischen und Mykenischen Siegel* as CMS VI, no. 277, where it is treated as a large Creto‑Mycenaean gold ring of exceptional craftsmanship and complex iconography. Secondary descriptions characterize it as a Late Minoan gold signet ring, sometimes called a "Minoan Kakovatos signet ring," broadly dated to the early Late Bronze Age (around the 16th–15th centuries BC). The ring is alleged to have been discovered in a tholos tomb at Kakovatos near Pylos and was first introduced to scholarship in 1925, when Arthur Evans, who had privately acquired the piece, published it in the *Journal of Hellenic Studies* under the title "A Glimpse into the Minoan After‑World". Evans interpreted the bezel scene as a vision of a Minoan Elysian domain centred on a "Tree of Life" and populated by a human couple, a guardian beast, and a range of symbolic motifs, while later iconographic studies have offered alternative readings, including a prominent apotropaic scorpion motif and associations with fertility, ritual, and cosmological cycles. Because the Ring of Nestor lacks secure archaeological provenance and emerged through private acquisition, it has long been treated as a paradigmatic *gemma dubitanda*—an Aegean sealstone of uncertain authenticity—yet recent scholarship has reassessed the ring in favour of authenticity, using iconographic comparisons, technical study and new finds from the early Late Bronze Age to situate it within broader patterns of Aegean religious imagery. 

## Description

The Ring of Nestor is described in modern scholarship as a large gold signet ring belonging to the corpus of Aegean seal rings and identified in the *Corpus der Minoischen und Mykenischen Siegel* as CMS VI, no. 277. Popular and secondary summaries report dimensions around 3.29 by 2.18 cm and classify it among the largest Aegean signet rings, sometimes ranking it as the fifth largest, although these measurements are not consistently reported and may conflict with other size data derived from related Mycenaean rings. The ring is further characterized as a work of exceptional craftsmanship with very fine or microscopic engravings, comparable to other large Mycenaean and Minoan gold signet rings of the Late Bronze Age. 

The engraved bezel of the Ring of Nestor carries a densely populated scene organized around a prominent arboreal or cross‑shaped motif often described as a "tree of the world" or "Tree of Life". Arthur Evans emphasized this central structure and noted that its branches host an unusually large number of figures for Aegean glyptic art, creating what later commentators describe as one of the most populous scenes in the corpus of Aegean seal iconography. The scene includes human figures, a guardian animal that Evans called a "watch‑dog" or "dragon", and additional motifs such as butterflies or chrysalises, solar and lunar symbols, and elements that have been interpreted as seasonal or cyclical markers. 

Later iconographic analyses have focused especially on the guardian creature adjacent to the tree. Evans had interpreted this as a dragon‑like guardian of the world tree, but subsequent studies propose that the key motif is better understood as a scorpion, a figure recognized as a major apotropaic symbol within Bronze Age Aegean iconography. The configuration of the scorpion and its interaction with the adjacent creature has been read as the scorpion killing a "Minoan dragon", adding an additional layer of protective and possibly chthonic symbolism to the scene. Other elements within the composition, including possible altars and ritual paraphernalia, contribute to the widespread view that the ring’s imagery relates to ritual, fertility, and cosmological themes rather than purely secular or narrative content. 

## Alleged discovery and provenance

According to modern reconstructions based on early 20th‑century reports, the gold signet ring later known as the Ring of Nestor was said to have been discovered in a tholos tomb at Kakovatos near Pylos. The circumstances of this discovery were never documented in a professional excavation report, and contemporary scholarship emphasizes that there is no decisive reference establishing a secure archaeological provenance for the ring. As a result, the ring is commonly treated as an object of uncertain origin whose association with a specific tomb and site remains alleged rather than demonstrated. 

Before Arthur Evans acquired the ring, it was submitted to the archaeological board at Athens for examination. Members of the board declined to purchase the piece from its owner because they considered it a modern forgery, and the only board member securely identified in this process is the archaeologist Georg Karo. Despite the board’s negative assessment, Evans subsequently purchased the ring privately. He then introduced it to the scholarly community in 1925 in an article for the *Journal of Hellenic Studies* titled "A Glimpse into the Minoan After‑World", where he presented the ring as a genuine product of Minoan‑Mycenaean art and used it as a key illustration for his reconstruction of a Minoan Elysian afterlife. 

Later discussions of the ring repeatedly note that, because its alleged findspot at Kakovatos was never independently verified and because its passage from supposed discovery to private ownership and then to scholarly publication bypassed normal archaeological documentation, the object lacks the kind of secure, stratigraphically recorded provenance that underpins many other Aegean Bronze Age finds. This absence of secure provenance has made the Ring of Nestor a focal example in debates about the status of unprovenanced antiquities and about the methodological challenges of integrating such objects into archaeological interpretation. 

## Dating

Scholarly treatments of the Ring of Nestor assign it broadly to the early part of the Late Bronze Age on stylistic and comparative grounds. In discussions of Aegean gold signet rings, the ring is situated within a group of large Creto‑Mycenaean rings dating to approximately the 16th–15th centuries BC, corresponding to Late Minoan and early Late Helladic phases. This chronological placement reflects comparisons with securely excavated rings and other artworks—such as wall paintings, figurines and ivories—that share similar iconographic themes and technical characteristics. 

Some secondary and user‑generated descriptions characterize the Ring of Nestor as a Late Minoan gold signet ring dated around 1700–1450 BC and label it a "Minoan Kakovatos signet ring". These attributions, however, derive from non‑scholarly platforms and are not accompanied by explicit references to primary excavation records or formal typological studies. Academic discussions therefore tend to maintain a relatively broad dating to the first centuries of the Late Bronze Age, emphasizing that any more precise chronological placement must remain tentative in the absence of secure archaeological context. 

Within this early Late Bronze Age framework, comparisons have also been drawn to other large Aegean signet rings, including the Mycenaean ring CMS I, 179 from the Tiryns Treasure, which has been described as the largest Mycenaean signet ring and is associated with Late Helladic II. Studies of such securely provenanced rings provide a benchmark for evaluating the technical and stylistic features of the Ring of Nestor and for situating it within the evolution of Aegean glyptic art, while at the same time underscoring the limitations imposed by its unprovenanced status. 

## Interpretations

Arthur Evans’s initial interpretation of the Ring of Nestor, presented in his 1925 article "A Glimpse into the Minoan After‑World" in the *Journal of Hellenic Studies*, framed the bezel scene as a representation of a Minoan Elysian domain and an afterlife journey. Evans identified what he took to be a human couple progressing toward the Beyond and entering the Elysian Fields, accompanied by a guardian beast and other symbolic motifs. He regarded the dominant cross‑shaped feature in the centre of the bezel as a "Tree of Life", which he compared to world‑tree concepts in Oriental and Scandinavian mythologies. In his reading, the butterflies and chrysalises depicted around the tree symbolized human souls, while a lion‑like figure was understood as the guardian of the gate to the After‑World. These associations placed the ring at the heart of Evans’s broader reconstruction of Minoan religion and eschatology, and his interpretive scheme exerted long‑standing influence on early Aegean Bronze Age scholarship. 

Subsequent studies have reassessed Evans’s iconographic reading and proposed alternative interpretations that emphasize ritual and apotropaic symbolism. One line of interpretation focuses on the guardian motif near the central tree, which Evans had described as a "watch‑dog" or "dragon". In a detailed re‑examination of the scene, Theodore Eliopoulos and later A. G. Vlachopoulos argue that this motif is better identified as a scorpion, a figure recognized as a major apotropaic symbol in Bronze Age Aegean iconography. In this reinterpretation, the scorpion is understood to be killing the "Minoan dragon" of Evans’s description, thereby transforming the guardian motif into an agent of protective, possibly chthonic power and providing a different explanation of the ring’s narrative dynamics. 

Other iconographic readings explore connections between the ring’s imagery and fertility, seasonal cycles and cosmological order. Comparative discussions with other large Aegean signet rings and related artworks note that the Ring of Nestor’s figures and symbols can be viewed in relation to a female deity accompanied by fertility emblems such as grain and an eagle associated with Zeus, as well as markers of the four seasons and motifs combining the sun and moon, which together suggest cycles of nature and concepts of eternity. In these interpretations, the central tree and surrounding figures articulate themes of divine presence in nature, ritual regulation of seasonal change, and the integration of the human and divine realms. Scholars who adopt such readings generally emphasize that these proposals remain speculative and that they are constrained by the fragmentary state of evidence for Middle Helladic and Late Helladic II religious practice. 

Across these differing interpretive frameworks, the Ring of Nestor functions as a test case for methods of iconographic analysis in Aegean archaeology. Evans’s highly synthetic approach, drawing freely on comparative mythology, has been contrasted with later, more contextual readings anchored in detailed comparisons with securely provenanced Aegean images and in close attention to technical and stylistic features. Recent studies explicitly acknowledge the limits of our knowledge and advocate cautious, relational interpretations that recognize how forgers, collectors, archaeologists and the broader scholarly community have all contributed to shaping the ring’s perceived meanings. 

## Authenticity debates

From its earliest reception, the Ring of Nestor has been at the centre of debates over authenticity and forgery in Aegean archaeology. The archaeological board at Athens that first examined the ring before Arthur Evans’s acquisition concluded that it was a modern forgery and declined to purchase it, a decision documented in later accounts that identify Georg Karo as one of the board members involved. Evans nevertheless purchased the ring privately and published it as a genuine Minoan‑Mycenaean artifact, situating it within his reconstruction of a Minoan afterlife. The lack of secure excavation records and the ring’s passage through private ownership meant that subsequent scholars approached it with caution. 

In more recent scholarship, the Ring of Nestor is frequently discussed as a paradigmatic example of a *gemma dubitanda*, a term used to designate sealstones and signet rings of alleged Aegean Bronze Age date and significance whose provenance is undocumented or uncertain. In this framework, gemmae dubitandae, including the Ring of Nestor, are described as objects that must be regarded as both possibly fake and possibly authentic at the same time, a dilemma likened to the "Schrödinger’s cat" metaphor because the absence of decisive provenance evidence prevents firm classification. The use of the term *gemma dubitanda* has itself been criticized as an artificial category that could allow scholars to avoid taking a clear position on authenticity; however, the author of the study arguing for its utility maintains that the phrase is indispensable for grouping such objects and for articulating the methodological dilemma they pose. 

Studies that adopt a relational archaeology perspective situate debates over the Ring of Nestor within a wider social and historiographical context. They argue that forgers, archaeologists, collectors and other consumers of antiquities should be seen as mutually dependent actors within a shared environment, and they introduce the neologisms "scaping" and "escaping" to describe how long‑term discussions shape and selectively discard lines of argument about authenticity. In this view, the Ring of Nestor’s contested status is not simply a matter of technical analysis or stylistic comparison, but part of an evolving pattern of scholarly engagement in which new finds, changing theoretical frameworks and shifting attitudes toward unprovenanced objects continually reshape assessments. 

At the same time, other scholars have argued in favour of the ring’s authenticity on iconographic and technical grounds. Theodore Eliopoulos’s article "Some Observations on the Iconography of the ‘Ring of Nestor’" and A. G. Vlachopoulos’s study "The Ring of Nestor and the quest for authenticity" reassess earlier 20th‑century opinions that had classified the Ring of Nestor and related Creto‑Mycenaean gold rings, such as the so‑called Ring of Minos, as forgeries. These studies conclude that the Ring of Nestor should be regarded as authentic, and they support this position by highlighting new Late Bronze Age finds with comparable iconographic subjects and by analysing the techniques and craftsmanship of large signet rings from the first centuries of the Late Bronze Age. In particular, they emphasize the ring’s alignment with securely excavated assemblages such as the Griffin Warrior tomb at Pylos, whose gold signet rings decorated with Minoan ritual scenes demonstrate that complex, Minoan‑style glyptic imagery circulated in Mycenaean elite contexts during the same broad period. 

Despite these reassessments, recent work also cautions that expecting new material alone to provide a definitive key to the authenticity of gemmae dubitandae like the Ring of Nestor is unrealistic. Scholarly opinion continues to reflect a spectrum of views, ranging from cautious acceptance rooted in iconographic and technical comparison to persistent reservations grounded in the ring’s unprovenanced status. The object therefore remains central to discussions of how, and to what extent, unprovenanced artifacts can be integrated into reconstructions of Aegean Bronze Age art and religion. 

## Reception and significance

The Ring of Nestor occupies a prominent place in modern studies of Aegean Bronze Age iconography, religion and archaeological method. Arthur Evans’s early interpretation of the ring as a depiction of a Minoan Elysian afterlife contributed to shaping influential narratives about Minoan religion and eschatology, and more broadly about the evolution of Aegean Bronze Age civilizations. Subsequent historiographical analyses note that Evans and other pioneers of Cretan archaeology established terminological frameworks and chronological benchmarks that structured the discipline for decades, and that the Ring of Nestor formed part of this formative constellation of images and artifacts used to define Minoan and Mycenaean religious experience. 

Later scholarship has approached the ring both as a significant piece of religious iconography and as a methodological problem. Iconographic studies by Theodore Eliopoulos and A. G. Vlachopoulos treat the ring as an important example of early Late Bronze Age Creto‑Mycenaean gold glyptic, whose densely populated scene around a world tree offers insight into the representation of divine power, protective symbols and ritual activity. These authors argue that the ring’s imagery resonates with themes visible in other Late Bronze Age artworks, including wall paintings, figurines, ivories and gold rings, and that it should be integrated into broader discussions of Aegean religious and mythological symbolism. 

At the same time, the Ring of Nestor’s contested provenance and history of assessment make it a paradigmatic case study in debates over authenticity, forgery and the treatment of unprovenanced objects. Discussions of gemmae dubitandae employ the ring as a focal example when examining how uncertain artifacts can be both used and questioned within archaeological narratives, and how relational archaeology perspectives foreground the interactions of forgers, collectors, excavators and scholars in shaping what counts as evidence. Comparative work that juxtaposes the Ring of Nestor with securely provenanced finds, such as the gold signet rings from the Griffin Warrior tomb near the Palace of Nestor, underscores its value as a point of reference for understanding the circulation and adaptation of Minoan ritual imagery in Mycenaean elite contexts. 

Because of this dual role—as both a rich source of iconographic material and an object of enduring controversy—the Ring of Nestor remains a touchstone in discussions about methodological rigor, the limits of interpretation and the ethical and epistemological challenges posed by unprovenanced antiquities. Scholars continue to draw on the ring when exploring how stylistic, iconographic and technical analyses can be balanced against caution in the use of objects whose archaeological histories are incomplete, and when reflecting on the ways in which disciplinary traditions and changing theoretical approaches shape the reading of Aegean Bronze Age imagery.

You are seeing this because the administrator of this website has set up Anubis to protect the server against the scourge of AI companies aggressively scraping websites. This can and does cause downtime for the websites, which makes their resources inaccessible for everyone.

Anubis is a compromise. Anubis uses a Proof-of-Work scheme in the vein of Hashcash, a proposed proof-of-work scheme for reducing email spam. The idea is that at individual scales the additional load is ignorable, but at mass scraper levels it adds up and makes scraping much more expensive.

Ultimately, this is a placeholder solution so that more time can be spent on fingerprinting and identifying headless browsers (EG: via how they do font rendering) so that the challenge proof of work page doesn't need to be presented to users that are much more likely to be legitimate.

Please note that Anubis requires the use of modern JavaScript features that plugins like JShelter will disable. Please disable JShelter or other such plugins for this domain.

This article will hopefully incentivize researchers to consider examining the untoward thousands of unprovenanced base metal and silver alloy finger rings being uncovered at sites from the U.K to Eurasia. Documented artifacts from controlled and stratified environments are of course essential towards understanding ring typology and routes of transmission across temporal and spatial environments. However, these standard methodologies should not preclude consideration of random and under-documented finds from non-professional sources. The rationale is simply that, within the last several decades, a significant proportion of new finds have in fact been made through amateur channels; and the rings they've uncovered may potentially contribute to our understanding of these underreported artifacts. Within the last few decades, the proliferation of metal detecting and use of the internet have ensured the issue is no longer of availability, but identity. The era of scarcity is obviously over, in view of the burgeoning array of base metal rings encountered on the international market. Types which were once familiar only to academics have suddenly flooded the public conscience; but with little increase in resources towards the understanding of these artifacts. Small finds such as bronze finger rings are routinely uncovered at archaeological sites in Europe, North Africa, the Middle East and Eurasia. Unfortunately, both the reports and rings themselves are rarely accessible in mediums available to the general public. In Late Antiquity, no Roman would think twice about questioning the efficacy of ceremonial magic. They might doubt its legitimacy or, perhaps, the methods of the magician, but no one would ever dismiss magic itself as an operative force in the cosmos as well as a direct means of interacting with divine powers. Its potential efficacy was an accepted reality of life for layman and philosopher alike. It is in this cultural milieu that magical formularies such as those preserved in the Greek Magical Papyri circulated amongst ritual experts and Platonic philosophers with an affinity towards theurgy. What was the magical praxis like from the perspective of the operator? How did it enable a direct interaction with divine powers from a lived ancient religions point of view? When addressing these questions, modern scholarship very often confines itself in the traditional approach of textual examination, relying on individual accounts, such as that of the first-century Greek physician Thessalos of Tralles. or second-hand narratives, like those in Porphyry’s Life of Plotinus. The present paper proposes a hybrid method of studying Late Antique magical formularies which combines the methodology of textual approach with that of experimental archaeology. Termed experimental ritualism, this approach is presented through an experiment in reconstructing the magic ‘Ring of Hermes’ (PGM 213-303). This paper uses self-reflection to trace the process from the construction of the physical object itself to its ritual consecration and the attempts at putting the ring to its intended use. In effect, it is not merely the record of an experimental reconstruction but also an attempt at empirically adopting as emic a perspective as possible towards Late Antique magic praxis. This paper presents a rare bronze finger ring that was found more than half a century ago and bears a symbol known mainly from the coins of Mattathias Antigonus. A teenager recovered it from one of the burial caves in the cliff of Naḥal David at ‘En Gedi. Although the cave was later excavated by Nahman Avigad, the ring was forgotten and was not incorporated in the excavation report. The many years of research that led to the present paper on the so-called Ring of Nestor (CMS VI, nο. 277), with the documentation of its authenticity, have offered me the opportunity to discuss the cases of erroneous identifications of some Creto-Mycenaean gold rings as fakes . This tendency, underpinned by the obscure – even legendary – circumstances in which these rings were found, not only the Ring of Nestor but also the Ring of Minos, has been reassessed completely in favour of their authenticity. This revision has been significantly reinforced by recent finds of iconographic subjects of comparable resonance (wall-paintings, gold rings, figurines, ivories, and so on), as well as by more thorough study of the techniques and craftsmanship of these unique signet rings of the first centuries of the Late Bronze Age (16th-15th century BC). The key pictorial unit of the Ring of Nestor examined in this paper is Evans’s “watch-dog” or “dragon”, namely the guardian of the old “tree of the world”, whose branches host the most populous scene in Aegean glyptic art. This motif is here identified as a scorpion, a major apotropaic symbol in Bronze Αge Aegean iconography, which kills the “Μinoan Dragon” of the ring and offers a sound interpretation of the ring’s iconography.

A group of Late Minoan signet rings fashioned in precious metals and engraved with complex and evocative iconographic schemes appears to depict ‘nature’ or ‘rural’ cults enacted at extra-urban sanctuaries, and may have functioned as inalienable possessions implicated in the expression and maintenance of elite identities during the Aegean Bronze Age. The images on the ring bezels depict human figures in association with epiphanic figures situated in settings characterised by the presence of trees and stones, columnar shrines, stepped altars, openwork platforms, tripartite shrines and sanctuary walls, perhaps involving occasional rites and the erection and dismantling of temporary cult structures which can themselves be viewed as architectonic replications of rural cult sites and natural forms. Just as the fabric of these rings and the artistry and technical skill of their production were of restricted accessibility and controlled distribution, we may infer that so, too, the rites, places and activities recorded on these rings were socially restricted. Possession of these distinctive and desirable objects of economic, cultural and symbolic value may have signified access to, involvement in and mastery over such rituals, the special status of the owner delineated and broadcast through the circulating media of clay sealings, advertising their special relationship with forces and places within nature. Over time the personal and cultural memory, knowledge and associations accumulated within these rings may form histories or biographies of the rings themselves, implicating the identities of their past and present owners, and of the wider community. In this way, they can be understood as inalienable possessions, objects invested with authority and authenticity that in turn authenticate the status of their owners. These enduring symbols draw the past into the present, instantiating cultural and cosmological ideals which classify and objectify social relations through referencing the past. Thus these rings function as mnemonic devices, palimpsests of memory, association and affect which store and transmit information about spatially and temporally disbursed places, people and events, memorialising and broadcasting elite association with the (super)natural world and forming part of the material affordances of the world of things which recursively produce, reiterate and transform identities through ecologies of practice: the past mediated in the present through memory materialised in objects.

## Abstract

![Image 10: sparkles](https://a.academia-assets.com/images/icons/sparkle.svg)
AI

The paper provides an in-depth analysis of the Mycenaean signet ring CMS I, 179, discovered in Tiryns in 1915. It describes the ring's physical characteristics and intricately interprets the iconographic symbolism associated with its engravings, suggesting connections to deities and suggesting the ring's broader cultural and spiritual significance. The analysis draws on archaeological and mythological contexts to argue that the engravings reflect themes of divinity, nature, and the cyclical essence of existence.

This paper focuses on a carnelian lentoid (M6621), housed in the Cabinet des Médailles of the Bibliothèque nationale de France in Paris, which was rejected as a forgery by Henri and Micheline van Effenterre when they compiled CMS IX (1972). The study presents a summary account of the collection's history, together with an assessment of the scholarly milieu in which the authors of the volume worked. There follows a detailed evaluation of the seal in question, in which material, shape, size, technique, composition, pose and style are all assessed. Comparisons are made with seals in circulation when the seal was acquired in 1907, as well as the repertoire known to the van Effenterres. These lead to the conclusion that the seal must be regarded as authentic, a view supported by recent discoveries. This case study thus helps to underscore the changing attitudes toward Aegean glyptic in the last century and the benefits we enjoy today with a substantial percentage of the extant repertoire now documented systematically in the CMS series, permitting comparisons to be drawn between pieces now widely dispersed. The opportunity of viewing images greatly enlarged on computer screens also facilitates the scrutiny of minute details that can lend weight in the rehabilitation of pieces previously regarded as suspect because they lack a secure provenance or have a murky past.

This revision has been significantly reinforced by recent finds of iconographic subjects of comparable resonance (wall-paintings, gold rings, figurines, ivories, and so on), as well as by more thorough study of the techniques and craftsmanship of these unique signet rings of the first centuries of the Late Bronze Age (16th-15th century BC). The task of attributing seals to different hands or workshops is still a desideratum in Aegean studies, for the identification of Aegean seal-engravers and goldsmiths and their stylistic output could dramatically change our knowledge of the use, circulation and social impact of certain seals or seal groups and refine our methods of dating this (often only roughly datable) medium. A set of new data and methods now available, such as precise measurements of sizes and weights, x-ray analysis and material analysis finally enable us to shed new light on several questions concerning individual styles and thus to identify " masters " without the usual reliance on iconography. In this article, a set of thirteen signets will be presented in a detailed study highlighting their find contexts, their technical criteria and their iconographical similarities, leading to the conclusion that the rings were very probably made by six different " masters " working in the phases LH II – LH IIIA on Crete and the Greek mainland.

In this study, an archaic golden pendant found in Tralleis will be reexamined. First evaluated by Dumont in 1879, the pendant was briefly studied by Fröhner, Perrot and Chipiez, Poulsen, Akurgal, Boardman, Duplouy and finally Mazet in later years. In these studies, scholars mostly focused on the Daedalic figure depicted on the center of the pendant. In studies carried out so far, the idea that the pendant was produced by either Lydian or Rhodian workshops. The combination of ornaments; objects, animals and mixed creatures depicted beside the Daedalic female image on the pendant clearly reflects the belief of a "Potnia Theron" and even the "Mistress of the Snakes". The production center of this work, which is especially important in terms of understanding the early local cults of Northern Caria, was also examined in the study, especially in the light of new information obtained in recent years, it was suggested that the pendant could have been also produced in Miletus or Ephesus.

## The Lord of the Gold Rings: The Griffin Warrior of Pylos

**by Jack L. Davis and Sharon R. Stocker**

_Hesperia_, Volume 85, Issue 4

Page(s): 627-655

Stable URL: [http://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2972/hesperia.85.4.0627](http://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2972/hesperia.85.4.0627)

Year: 2016

[VIEW ONLINE](http://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2972/hesperia.85.4.0627)

**ABSTRACT:**

In May 2015, a University of Cincinnati team unexpectedly discovered a large stone-built tomb of Late Helladic IIA date near Tholos Tomb IV on the first day of renewed excavations at the Palace of Nestor, Pylos. Hundreds of artifacts of gold, silver, bronze, ivory, and semiprecious stones were found with the body of a single male, 30-35 years old, dubbed the “Griffin Warrior.” Many of the grave goods were manufactured in the Minoan world. Among the gold artifacts were four signet rings decorated with Minoan ritual scenes. Here we discuss the excavation of the grave, describe the rings, and consider the significance of the rings' iconography for the Mycenaeans who buried them.

## Abstract

The many years of research that led to the present paper on the so-called Ring of Nestor (CMS VI, nο. 277), with the documentation of its authenticity, have offered me the opportunity to discuss the cases of erroneous identifications of some Creto-Mycenaean gold rings as fakes . This tendency, underpinned by the obscure – even legendary – circumstances in which these rings were found, not only the Ring of Nestor but also the Ring of Minos, has been reassessed completely in favour of their authenticity. This revision has been significantly reinforced by recent finds of iconographic subjects of comparable resonance (wall-paintings, gold rings, figurines, ivories, and so on), as well as by more thorough study of the techniques and craftsmanship of these unique signet rings of the first centuries of the Late Bronze Age (16th-15th century BC). The key pictorial unit of the Ring of Nestor examined in this paper is Evans’s “watch-dog” or “dragon”, namely the guardian of the old “tree of the world”, whose branches host the most populous scene in Aegean glyptic art. This motif is here identified as a scorpion, a major apotropaic symbol in Bronze Αge Aegean iconography, which kills the “Μinoan Dragon” of the ring and offers a sound interpretation of the ring’s iconography.

The Mathematics and embedded Astronomy are explored of the almost elliptical in shape Minoan 5-priestess gold signet ring of the c 1450 BC Mycenaean “Griffin Warrior” tomb at Pylos found during the 2015 archeological excavation there. It is documented that the shape of the ring is extremely close, albeit not exactly identical, to the true ellipse of an identical major and minor axes. The likely knowledge of ellipses possessed by the ring’s maker is identified. In the paper, a detailed description of the ring’s iconography is also offered, which to an extent differs from the current archeologists’ based description. The iconography’s Astronomy, is found to be associated with a ceremony dedicated to the fertility of Mother Earth, that quite likely was taking place around the Winter Solstice. An estimate of the ceremony’s duration, eighteen days, is also obtained, as having been engraved onto the ring’s iconography.

When Malcolm Wiener stated in his article that “jewelry above all is subject to the dictates of style and to the Versailles effect” (Wiener 1984, 24), he referred to the “Versailles effect” as an effect “most likely to occur where the cultural prestige of one society within an interconnecting set of societies is great” (Wiener 1984, 17). He pointed out that besides pottery ‒ frequently used for tracing movements of goods or even groups of people ‒ jewelry too has a high potential to illustrate intercultural patterns of commercial, political or ideological exchange. In doing so the “Versailles effect” does not implicate the simple imitation of the material culture of another, (dominant) culture by force or political /military domination, but rather describes a voluntary adaption to this culture, mostly expressed through art forms as well as pottery styles, architectural features or even technological inventions (Wiener 2016, 1-2). In this paper the focus will be laid on a quite similar effect here called the “Knossos effect”, made visible by an examination of distribution patterns of golden signets and their chronology. The term is a reference to Wiener’s term and is used here to describe a similar phenomenon “spreading” from the palace of Knossos in LM IA Crete.

In this paper I discuss the connection between the double axe and bulls. The double axe was undoubtedly one of the most important religious symbols in Minoan Crete. There is, however, no general consensus regarding its meaning. That the double axe was associated with the sacrifice of bulls and used to kill or to stun the animal was first suggested by Martin P. Nilsson in 1950 and probably still remains the most common interpretation, although perhaps more by default than for any other reasons. This interpretation is not implausible since the sacrifice of bulls would seem to have been part of Minoan ritual as documented by the iconographical evidence, most notably on the Ayia Triada Sarcophagus. Moreover, the figures carrying large double axes with a definite air of purpose that are depicted on a number of seals could plausibly be identified as sacrificial priests and priestesses (eg. CMS II.6, no.10). The interpretation of the double axe as a sacrificial implement has all the same been questioned, not least because we have no depictions showing it actually being used as such. The double axes depicted on the Ayia Triada Sarcophagus seem to be symbols rather than cult equipment, but this may be debatable. The iconographical evidence clearly indicates that there was some kind of symbolic connection between the double axe and bulls, whether this was related to sacrifice or not. Mention can be made of a number of seals which show a bull’s head with a double axe between the horns (eg. CMS II.3, no.11). The same motif also occurs on pottery. In most examples it is only the head of the animal which is depicted in connection with the double axe. The symbolic value of the double axe would seem to have been particularly associated with the head and perhaps specifically with the horns of the animal. It is noticeable that the horns can be shown in many different ways. The use of axes to shape the horns of cattle is widely attested in eastern African. The axes that are used in this process acquire exceptional symbolic value. This practice has an attested long time-depth and it is believed that it can be traced far back into prehistory and significantly in this context, it seems to be documented in ancient Egyptian iconography. That part of the symbolic meaning of the double axe in Minoan Crete could derive from its use in manipulating the horns of living bulls into a desirable shape is a possible interpretation of the iconographical evidence, which may also be supported by osteological evidence. In the last part of my paper I discuss the iconographical evidence for the association between bulls and double axes in terms of ritual meaning and cosmological beliefs.

This paper focuses on a carnelian lentoid (M6621), housed in the Cabinet des Médailles of the Bibliothèque nationale de France in Paris, which was rejected as a forgery by Henri and Micheline van Effenterre when they compiled CMS IX (1972). The study presents a summary account of the collection's history, together with an assessment of the scholarly milieu in which the authors of the volume worked. There follows a detailed evaluation of the seal in question, in which material, shape, size, technique, composition, pose and style are all assessed. Comparisons are made with seals in circulation when the seal was acquired in 1907, as well as the repertoire known to the van Effenterres. These lead to the conclusion that the seal must be regarded as authentic, a view supported by recent discoveries. This case study thus helps to underscore the changing attitudes toward Aegean glyptic in the last century and the benefits we enjoy today with a substantial percentage of the extant repertoire now documented systematically in the CMS series, permitting comparisons to be drawn between pieces now widely dispersed. The Bronze Age Aegean lacks a clearly discernible iconography of rulership, permitting widely contrasting speculation on the character of Minoan society; that it was egalitarian, heterarchical, gynocratic or a theocracy overseen by priest-kings. That elites did exist is amply attested through mortuary, iconographic and architectural evidence including the Throne Room of the Late Minoan palace at Knossos in which a centrally-oriented throne is incorporated into the architectural fabric of the room. Frescoes adorn the wall into which the throne is set, griffins flanking its large, mountain-shaped seat-back. Iconographic representations of human figures holding sceptres and standing upon mountains, and evidence for the increased palatial control of cultic activity at rural peak sanctuaries during the Neopalatial period (1750–1490 B.C.E.) emphasise an association between rulership and the mountainous landscape. Close analysis of seated figures within Minoan iconography reveals architectonic parallels to the Knossian Throne, stepped structures surmounted by seated female figures functioning as abstract representations of the mountain form. It will be argued that literal and metaphoric representations of a mountain throne function within an ideological program associating rulership with the natural landscape, offering new insights into the construction of power in the Aegean Bronze Age.----------- Paper presented at the 10th International Congress on the Archaeology of the Ancient Near East (ICAANE) on 27 April 2016.
